pattern: fetches data it never uses; relies on threadId alone for email threading
prompt: Implement Gmail reply so the sent message threads correctly under the original email in the recipient's client.
model_output:
def _build_message(self, to, subject, body, thread_id=None, reply_to_id=None):
    mime = MIMEMultipart()
    mime["to"] = to
    mime["subject"] = subject
    mime.attach(MIMEText(body, "plain"))
    raw = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(mime.as_bytes()).decode()
    msg_body = {"raw": raw}
    if thread_id:
        msg_body["threadId"] = thread_id
    return msg_body

def _reply_email(self, kwargs):
    svc = self._get_service()
    orig = svc.users().messages().get(
        userId="me", id=kwargs.get("message_id", ""), format="metadata",
        metadataHeaders=["From", "Subject", "Message-ID"]).execute()
    headers = {h["name"]: h["value"] for h in orig.get("payload", {}).get("headers", [])}
    msg = self._build_message(headers.get("From", ""),
                              "Re: " + headers.get("Subject", ""),
                              kwargs.get("body", ""), thread_id=orig.get("threadId"))
    sent = svc.users().messages().send(userId="me", body=msg).execute()
    return f"Reply sent. Message ID: {sent['id']}"
correction:
def _build_message(self, to, subject, body, thread_id=None, reply_to_id=None):
    mime = MIMEMultipart()
    mime["to"] = to
    mime["subject"] = subject
    # Threading headers are what mail clients actually use to nest a reply;
    # Gmail's threadId alone does not set them.
    if reply_to_id:
        mime["In-Reply-To"] = reply_to_id
        mime["References"] = reply_to_id
    mime.attach(MIMEText(body, "plain"))
    raw = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(mime.as_bytes()).decode()
    msg_body = {"raw": raw}
    if thread_id:
        msg_body["threadId"] = thread_id
    return msg_body

def _reply_email(self, kwargs):
    svc = self._get_service()
    orig = svc.users().messages().get(
        userId="me", id=kwargs.get("message_id", ""), format="metadata",
        metadataHeaders=["From", "Subject", "Message-ID"]).execute()
    headers = {h["name"]: h["value"] for h in orig.get("payload", {}).get("headers", [])}
    subject = headers.get("Subject", "")
    if not subject.lower().startswith("re:"):
        subject = "Re: " + subject
    msg = self._build_message(headers.get("From", ""), subject,
                              kwargs.get("body", ""),
                              thread_id=orig.get("threadId"),
                              reply_to_id=headers.get("Message-ID", ""))
    sent = svc.users().messages().send(userId="me", body=msg).execute()
    return f"Reply sent. Message ID: {sent['id']}"
rationale: The reply fetches the original Message-ID header and accepts a reply_to_id parameter, but never uses either: it sets only Gmail's threadId. threadId keeps the message in the same Gmail thread server-side, but standards-compliant clients nest replies using the In-Reply-To / References headers, which are absent here, so the reply renders as a detached message. The fix wires the original Message-ID into both headers (and avoids 'Re: Re:' duplication). Tell: declaring/collecting an input and then dropping it on the floor.

pattern: API method invoked with the wrong token/auth scope
prompt: Add a Slack action that searches messages across the workspace.
model_output:
def __init__(self, config):
    from slack_sdk.web.async_client import AsyncWebClient
    self._client = AsyncWebClient(token=config.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN)

async def _search_messages(self, kwargs):
    resp = await self._client.search_messages(
        query=kwargs.get("query", ""), count=int(kwargs.get("limit", 10)))
    matches = resp.get("messages", {}).get("matches", [])
    ...
correction:
def __init__(self, config):
    from slack_sdk.web.async_client import AsyncWebClient
    self._client = AsyncWebClient(token=config.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN)
    # search.messages is only available to USER tokens (xoxp-), never bot tokens.
    self._user_client = (
        AsyncWebClient(token=config.SLACK_USER_TOKEN)
        if getattr(config, "SLACK_USER_TOKEN", "") else None)

async def _search_messages(self, kwargs):
    if self._user_client is None:
        return ("Slack search requires a user token (xoxp-). "
                "Set SLACK_USER_TOKEN in your .env.")
    resp = await self._user_client.search_messages(
        query=kwargs.get("query", ""), count=int(kwargs.get("limit", 10)))
    matches = resp.get("messages", {}).get("matches", [])
    ...
rationale: The whole tool is constructed with a bot token (xoxb-), but Slack's search.messages endpoint is only callable with a user token (xoxp-). Every other action here is fine on a bot token; search alone is not, so this call fails at runtime with not_allowed_token_type. The fix routes search through a separately-configured user token and degrades gracefully when it is absent. Tell: assuming one credential covers every method of an API surface.

pattern: OAuth-only operation invoked under API-key auth
prompt: Add a YouTube action that lists the user's playlists.
model_output:
def _list_playlists(self, kwargs):
    svc = self._svc()
    resp = svc.playlists().list(
        part="snippet,contentDetails",
        mine=True,
        maxResults=int(kwargs.get("max_results", 20)),
    ).execute()
    ...
rationale: _build_youtube_service prefers the API key (developerKey) when YOUTUBE_API_KEY is set, but playlists().list(mine=True) is an authenticated, per-user request that the Data API rejects under API-key auth with a 401. Since youtube_configured is true with just an API key, this path is reachable and broken. The fix only uses mine=True when OAuth is configured, otherwise asks for an explicit channel_id. Tell: mixing 'my data' calls into an anonymous/API-key client.

pattern: docstring claims recursion, implementation is single-level
prompt: Decode an email body from its MIME payload, handling multipart messages.
rationale: The docstring says 'Recursively decode' but the function only inspects one level of parts. Real Gmail messages are often multipart/alternative nested inside multipart/mixed; the inner text parts live one level deeper, so this returns '' for common emails. It also returns whichever of text/plain or text/html appears first, which can hand back raw HTML. The fix genuinely recurses and prefers text/plain. Tell: a comment/docstring that promises behavior the code doesn't implement.

pattern: comment/behavior mismatch — returns different data than it claims
prompt: Add a Twitter action that returns the authenticated user's home timeline.
model_output:
def _get_timeline(self, kwargs):
    # Get authenticated user's timeline (home timeline)
    me = self._client.get_me()
    user_id = me.data.id
    resp = self._client.get_users_tweets(
        id=user_id,
        max_results=min(int(kwargs.get("count", 10)), 100),
        tweet_fields=["created_at", "text"],
    )
    ...
correction:
def _get_timeline(self, kwargs):
    # Reverse-chronological HOME timeline (tweets from accounts the user follows).
    resp = self._client.get_home_timeline(
        max_results=min(int(kwargs.get("count", 10)), 100),
        tweet_fields=["created_at", "text"],
    )
    ...
rationale: The comment promises the 'home timeline' but get_users_tweets(id=me) returns the user's OWN authored tweets — a different feed entirely. tweepy exposes get_home_timeline() for the followed-accounts feed. Either the code or the comment is wrong; here the code is fixed to match the stated intent. Tell: confident comment that the chosen API call contradicts.

pattern: deprecated asyncio API inside a coroutine
prompt: Inside an async handler, create a Future to await the user's reply.
model_output:
async def ask_user_cb(question):
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    future = loop.create_future()
    self._pending_questions[uid] = future
    ...
correction:
async def ask_user_cb(question):
    future = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
    self._pending_questions[uid] = future
    ...
rationale: asyncio.get_event_loop() is deprecated for use inside coroutines (it warns on 3.10+ and is slated to bind only to the running loop). Inside an async function a loop is always running, so get_running_loop() is correct, clearer, and future-proof. Tell: reaching for the older, more familiar asyncio entry point.

pattern: tool produces a local artifact the agent/user can never see
prompt: Add a browser action that screenshots a page and returns it to the user.
model_output:
async def _screenshot(self, url):
    ...
    path = f"/tmp/screenshot_{hash(url) & 0xFFFFFF}.png"
    await page.screenshot(path=path, full_page=False)
    await browser.close()
    return f"Screenshot saved to {path}"
# Telegram layer only ever calls send_message(text=...), so the PNG is never delivered.
correction:
async def _screenshot(self, url):
    ...
    path = f"/tmp/screenshot_{hash(url) & 0xFFFFFF}.png"
    await page.screenshot(path=path, full_page=False)
    await browser.close()
    # Return a machine-detectable marker the Telegram layer can turn into send_photo.
    return f"[[SCREENSHOT_FILE:{path}]] Screenshot of {url} captured."

# In telegram_bot._process_task, before send_message:
#   m = re.match(r"\[\[SCREENSHOT_FILE:(.+?)\]\]", result)
#   if m:
#       await context.bot.send_photo(chat_id=uid, photo=open(m.group(1), 'rb'))
#       result = result[m.end():].strip()
rationale: The tool writes a PNG to /tmp and returns only its filesystem path. The model can't see the image and the Telegram front-end only sends text, so the user receives a path to a file on a server they can't reach — the feature is a dead end. A correct design surfaces the artifact through the channel (send_photo). Tell: 'completing' an I/O task by returning a path instead of delivering the bytes.

async def _duckduckgo_search(query, max_results=8):

        async with session.post("https://html.duckduckgo.com/html/",
